title: Massachusetts v. Environmental Protection Agency
lead: A petition about vehicle emissions reaches the Supreme Court through a divided appellate court, requiring a decision about Massachusetts’s right to sue before the Environmental Protection Agency’s reasons for refusing regulation can be tested.

actors.name: Nineteen private organizations
actors.role: Filed the 1999 administrative petition concerning four greenhouse gases from new motor vehicles.

actors.name: Massachusetts
actors.role: State petitioner owning coastal land; its asserted injury supplied the majority’s basis for standing.

actors.name: Environmental Protection Agency
actors.role: Agency that denied the petition on statutory-authority and discretionary-policy grounds.

actors.name: Other States, local governments, and organizations
actors.role: Joined the judicial-review petition; other States and industry associations intervened to support EPA.

proceedings: EPA solicited comments in 2001 and denied the petition on September 8, 2003.
The D.C. Circuit denied review through three separate judicial positions.
The Supreme Court reversed and remanded on April 2, 2007, by a 5–4 vote.
limits: The scientific quantities and agency positions describe the 2007 record. The Court neither made an endangerment finding nor ordered particular standards. Later regulation and changes in deference doctrine are separate matters. Assigned merits-note pages 1080–1085 were unavailable; the four standing notes were complete.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: An emissions statute supplies the route to a petition
sections.cue: What question had Congress assigned EPA to answer?
paragraphs: Massachusetts owned coastal property threatened by rising seas. Its later affidavits described twentieth-century sea-level increases, existing coastal loss, and future inundation and storm-surge risks. Scientific assessments connected accumulating greenhouse gases with warming and associated harms. The parties would dispute whether the particular federal failure to regulate emissions from new vehicles was sufficiently linked to Massachusetts's land loss and whether regulation could reduce that risk. These were the record's claims and evidence, not an undisputed finding about every predicted loss.

The Clean Air Act placed responsibility for new-motor-vehicle emissions with the Environmental Protection Agency. Section 202(a)(1) required the Administrator to prescribe standards when, in the Administrator’s judgment, the emissions cause or contribute to air pollution reasonably anticipated to endanger public health or welfare. The statutory definition of “air pollutant” included physical, chemical, biological, or radioactive substances entering ambient air, and “welfare” expressly included weather and climate effects. Section 7607(b)(1) supplied judicial review of the agency action at issue.

On October 20, 1999, nineteen private organizations petitioned EPA to regulate carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, and hydrofluorocarbons from new motor vehicles. The organizations invoked scientific assessments of warming and associated harms. They also relied on EPA’s own legal views: General Counsel Jonathan Cannon had accepted authority over carbon dioxide in 1998, and his successor Gary Guzy reiterated that view in 1999. The administrative petitioners must be distinguished from the broader coalition, including Massachusetts, that later sought judicial review.

EPA requested public comment in 2001 and received more than 50,000 comments. At the White House’s request, the National Research Council prepared a report describing accumulating greenhouse gases, increasing temperatures, and uncertainties about future magnitude and effects. EPA and the petitioners would draw different conclusions from that report about whether the available science permitted a statutory judgment.

sources.pinpoint: 549 U.S. at 505–512; Statutory framework; Material facts and administrative proceedings

sections.title: EPA gives two independent reasons for refusing
sections.cue: Why would a ruling about statutory authority alone not resolve the petition?
paragraphs: EPA denied the petition on September 8, 2003. Its first ground was that the Clean Air Act did not authorize mandatory regulation of greenhouse gases to address global climate change. EPA pointed to the history of climate legislation, Congress’s failure to enact a proposed emissions amendment, the economic and political importance of the subject, the Act’s traditional treatment of local air pollution, and the Department of Transportation’s fuel-economy responsibilities.

EPA separately said that it would decline to regulate even if authority existed. The agency invoked scientific uncertainty, coordinated rather than piecemeal action, voluntary programs and technological innovation, and a concern that unilateral domestic regulation would impede obtaining reductions from developing countries. Thus, the petitioners eventually had to overcome both the no-authority rationale and the alternative exercise-of-discretion rationale. They sought lawful consideration under § 202, not judicial authorship of emissions standards.

sources.pinpoint: 549 U.S. at 512–514; Parties and requested relief

sections.title: Massachusetts joins the court challenge and the appellate judges divide
sections.cue: Who said what in the D.C. Circuit?
paragraphs: Massachusetts joined other States, local governments, and private organizations in challenging the denial. EPA defended its decision with support from intervening States and industry associations. Massachusetts submitted affidavits about its ownership of coastal property, twentieth-century sea-level increases, existing coastal loss, and future inundation and storm-surge risks. Those submissions would become central to a disputed jurisdictional question: whether the particular omission concerning new-vehicle standards caused a sufficiently concrete and redressable injury.

The D.C. Circuit denied the petition for review, but its judges supplied three different positions. Judge Randolph assumed regulatory authority without deciding it and accepted EPA’s policy grounds. Randolph also avoided a definitive standing ruling because he considered standing and the merits intertwined. Judge Sentelle thought the injury insufficient for standing; accepting the contrary standing position as law of the case, he joined the merits judgment as the disposition closest to his own position.

Judge Tatel dissented. He found Massachusetts’s affidavits sufficient on injury, causation, and redressability, read the statute to authorize regulation, and rejected EPA’s policy grounds for declining the statutory inquiry. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and heard argument on November 29, 2006. It first had to resolve Article III jurisdiction before reaching EPA’s authority and reasons.

sections.title: The majority connects a review right with threatened state property
sections.cue: Why did Massachusetts receive special solicitude without eliminating concrete injury?
paragraphs: Justice Stevens wrote for Justices Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer. Because one petitioner with standing was enough, the majority focused on Massachusetts; it did not decide whether every member of the coalition could sue. A statutory procedural right protecting a concrete interest can relax the usual demands concerning immediacy and certainty of redress. Lawful reconsideration need only have some possibility of reducing the injury even though the agency retains substantive discretion. An abstract interest in correct government administration remains insufficient.

Massachusetts had both substantial coastal property and an independent interest in its territory and environmental conditions. Drawing on Georgia v. Tennessee Copper, the majority observed that States surrendered powers over war, international treaties, and some regulation when entering the Union. Federal authority occupied that space, and Congress had assigned EPA protective duties. The combination of state interests and the statutory review right warranted special solicitude.

The majority distinguished Massachusetts v. Mellon: Massachusetts was seeking to vindicate rights under an existing federal statute, rather than representing citizens against the operation of federal law. It also distinguished a widely shared injury from an abstract public interest. Many people could suffer climate-related harm while this particular State suffered concrete loss of property. The affidavits supported existing and continuing land loss without identifying the exact metes and bounds of every affected parcel. The majority’s use of the evidence was contested, not an uncontested determination of every predicted loss.

sources.pinpoint: 549 U.S. at 516–523, 520–521 n.17, 523 n.21; Majority reasoning; Complete opinion and footnote clarifications

sections.title: The majority accepts contribution and incremental relief
sections.cue: How could regulation matter if it could not solve global warming?
paragraphs: EPA did not dispute the causal connection between human greenhouse-gas emissions and warming. It argued instead that the emissions covered by this petition contributed too little to support standing. The majority answered that agencies commonly address large problems through partial measures. The 2007 record described U.S. transportation emissions of approximately 1.7 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide in 1999, more than six percent of the worldwide total. That contribution was not insignificant.

Relief did not have to reverse global warming. Reducing or slowing the risk to Massachusetts could count. Expected increases in foreign emissions did not erase the possible benefit of domestic reductions; EPA’s own support for voluntary reductions assumed that lowering emissions could help. The majority therefore found a sufficient prospect that lawful reconsideration would lead to measures reducing the State’s risk.

The figures concerned the transportation sector as a whole. As the standing dissent emphasized, the statutory category of new vehicles and the reductions attainable through actual standards were narrower. The majority and dissent differed over the sufficiency of this causal and remedial connection. The majority did not promise that the petitioners would receive a particular regulation or prove that regulation alone would save all threatened property.

sources.pinpoint: 549 U.S. at 523–526, 543–545; Majority reasoning: Contribution and incremental mitigation

sections.title: The Court permits review and reads the grant of authority
sections.cue: Why did nonenforcement doctrine and the absence of a climate amendment not control?
paragraphs: With standing established, the majority distinguished Heckler v. Chaney, which concerned individual nonenforcement. This petition sought rulemaking through a congressionally supplied review procedure. Rulemaking denials were less frequent, involved formal procedures, and produced public explanations that courts could compare with statutory requirements. Review remained narrow and highly deferential, but EPA’s refusal was reviewable.

The four gases fell within the Act’s broad definition of air pollutant: they were physical or chemical substances emitted into ambient air and acted in producing the pollution at issue. Statutory breadth could encompass developments Congress had not specifically anticipated. The majority did not treat breadth as an ambiguity requiring deference to EPA’s restrictive view.

Later legislation emphasizing climate research did not withdraw authority already granted, and failure to enact a proposed emissions amendment did not establish that the existing general language lacked coverage. EPA needed a statutory restriction, not an inference from Congress’s failure to adopt a later, more specific mandate.

sources.pinpoint: 549 U.S. at 527–530, 532; Majority reasoning: rulemaking denial and statutory definition

sections.title: Other agencies and presidential policy do not displace EPA’s assignment
sections.cue: How did the Court distinguish tobacco regulation and fuel economy?
paragraphs: EPA invoked FDA v. Brown & Williamson, but the majority found the analogy unpersuasive. There, the FDA’s asserted reading would have required a tobacco ban against a distinctive history of congressional protection of tobacco and agency disclaimers of authority. Regulation under § 202 did not require a comparable ban. The Clean Air Act accommodated technological development and time, and EPA’s earlier counsel had accepted greenhouse-gas authority.

The Department of Transportation’s fuel-economy mandate concerned energy efficiency, while EPA’s mandate concerned emissions affecting health and welfare. Increased fuel economy might reduce emissions, but overlapping responsibilities were not incompatible legal commands. EPA still had to carry out its own statute.

The Administrator’s “judgment” concerned the scientific and statutory endangerment question. It did not authorize replacing that inquiry with presidential preferences, diplomatic strategy, or a preference for a different regulatory sequence. The majority recognized presidential foreign-affairs authority but held that it did not excuse nonexecution of domestic law. Congress had assigned the relevant foreign-policy role to the State Department, and EPA had not shown consultation with that department.

sources.pinpoint: 549 U.S. at 530–535; Majority reasoning; Complete opinion and footnote clarifications

sections.title: The majority requires an explanation and sends the petition back
sections.cue: What remained for EPA to decide?
paragraphs: Scientific uncertainty could justify declining an endangerment judgment if EPA explained why the uncertainty prevented a reasoned determination. EPA could also find that the statutory endangerment condition was absent. The majority found that EPA’s actual discussion of residual uncertainty and its unrelated policy concerns did not adequately answer the question Congress assigned.

On April 2, 2007, the Court reversed the D.C. Circuit and remanded for proceedings consistent with its opinion. EPA could no longer rely on the rejected absence-of-authority rationale or the unrelated policy reasons as sufficient explanations. EPA retained responsibility for a reasoned scientific judgment and for the manner and timing of regulation within the Act. The Court neither found endangerment nor ordered immediate standards, and expressly reserved whether policy concerns might inform agency action after an endangerment finding.

sections.title: Roberts would have ended the case for lack of standing
sections.cue: Which links in Massachusetts’s jurisdictional showing did the Chief Justice dispute?
paragraphs: Chief Justice Roberts dissented, joined by Justices Scalia, Thomas, and Alito. Roberts would have vacated the appellate judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction. That proposed disposition was different from affirming EPA on the merits.

Roberts rejected special solicitude. Tennessee Copper concerned the substantive and remedial significance of state interests, not relaxation of Article III. State ownership resembled any landowner’s proprietary interest; an additional quasi-sovereign theory raised the problem of a State suing the federal government as representative of its citizens. A general review provision could not cure constitutional deficiencies.

Roberts considered the assertions of already submerged state land too conclusory, and the future projections too dependent on distant time horizons and uncertain assumptions. He compared projected sea-level change with the limitations of the elevation measurements used to identify threatened property. His objection concerned proof of injury in this record, not a categorical denial that environmental injury could be concrete.

He then traced the chain from EPA’s refusal through new-vehicle emissions, atmospheric concentration, temperature, sea level, and particular Massachusetts land. He stressed the gap between total transportation emissions and attainable regulatory reductions, alongside foreign emissions, natural processes, and future behavior. In his view, the resulting benefit was too speculative. His discussion and notes criticized SCRAP’s attenuated causation and imminence and insisted that a serious policy problem or political inaction could not enlarge judicial power.

sources.pinpoint: 549 U.S. at 535–549, 540 n.1, 548 n.2; Separate opinions: Roberts

sections.title: Scalia offers three additional grounds for sustaining EPA
sections.cue: How were timing, scientific explanation, and statutory definition distinct objections?
paragraphs: Justice Scalia joined Roberts’s jurisdictional dissent and wrote a second dissent, also joined by Roberts, Thomas, and Alito, assuming jurisdiction for purposes of addressing the merits. Scalia read the Administrator’s judgment as a condition for mandatory regulation, not an unconditional obligation to make an endangerment determination whenever someone petitioned. EPA could reasonably decide when to undertake that judgment and could consider surrounding policy and administrative factors. His timing argument distinguished deferring the inquiry from the eventual regulatory decision.

Even accepting the majority’s narrower limits, Scalia found EPA’s scientific explanation adequate. He relied on the agency’s discussion of unresolved emissions questions, atmospheric responses, feedback effects, and health and welfare consequences. EPA had supplied an explanation; he disagreed with the majority about its sufficiency.

Scalia separately challenged the air-pollutant definition. The opening category, an “air pollution agent,” constrained the examples following “including.” Being physical or chemical matter did not automatically establish membership in the opening category. His analogy was that American automobiles, including trucks and minivans, would not thereby include foreign trucks. Because the Act did not separately define air pollution, he would have deferred under the then-operative Chevron framework to EPA’s distinction between global greenhouse effects and ordinary ambient-air pollution. These were alternative statutory grounds, not Roberts’s standing analysis or a statement of present deference law.

sources.pinpoint: 549 U.S. at 549–560, 551 n.1, 558 n.2; Separate opinions: Scalia

sections.title: The assigned notes follow the decision into questions about review and standing
sections.cue: Which observations belong to the editors and later commentators?
paragraphs: The casebook places this same decision in administrative review and standing. Its available merits notes, at pages 1077–1079, discuss scarce resources, priority setting, and undeveloped records as explanations for narrow review. The editors compare Lyng’s developed record and explanatory remand with their accounts of Conservancy of Southwest Florida, New York v. NRC, and Flyers Rights. They also describe a 2008 advance notice after this decision. Those comparisons and later events are editorial material, not additional Massachusetts holdings or independently audited accounts of the other cases.

The next available merits note considers APA §§ 553(e), 555(e), 551, and 702. A petition can request a proceeding not yet begun, and a duty to state reasons does not by itself resolve reviewability. The supplied pages then jump from 1079 to 1086. The later Farmworker Justice fragment cannot establish what the missing pages 1080–1085 contained or how many Massachusetts-related notes were omitted.

The four complete standing notes, pages 1239–1243, explore a possible public-action/SCRAP reading without eliminating the concrete-injury requirement; whether the review provision supplies the relevant procedural right; comparisons to Spokeo and TransUnion; and whether existing harm or increased future risk does the work. The quoted Lujan dam example appears at 573 n.7 in the original report, although the note prints 572 n.7.

The final standing note compares proprietary, sovereign, and quasi-sovereign interests. It labels Freeman and Vermeule’s political-expertise explanation as speculation and presents Merrill’s state-court theory alongside Percival’s and Watts and Wildermuth’s federalism accounts. It also considers elected attorneys general and private public-interest representatives. These are scholarly positions, not findings about the Justices’ motives.

The editors’ later-case comparisons include unsuccessful state standing arguments in Trump v. New York, California v. Texas, and Texas v. Pennsylvania; the MOHELA-based injury and dissenting third-party objection in Biden v. Nebraska; and United States v. Texas. In the last comparison, the five-Justice rulemaking/enforcement rationale differs from the three-Justice concurrence’s criticism of special solicitude. That criticism is not an express holding overruling Massachusetts. A separate page gap, 1244–1249, concerns the ensuing zone-of-interests/Air Courier material rather than these complete four notes.
